claims.text: The proposed framework integrates DFT-derived electron–phonon scattering parameters with on-the-fly machine-learned force fields.
The framework will separately calculate electronic and lattice thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The separate conductivity predictions will be quantitatively accurate.
Predicted total thermal conductivity will fall within 10–17 W/(K m).
Prediction error will be reduced by approximately 20% relative to traditional approaches.
The relevant initial material is nominally single-phase bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The material may contain as much as 1 wt.% oxygen.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
The proposed applicability range is approximately 50–1200 K.
DFT-resolved local electron density and phonon dispersion mediate electron–phonon scattering and lattice vibrations.
Independently resolving electron and phonon scattering will capture atomic-scale thermal-transport complexity more effectively than simplified analytical treatments.
The framework will capture temperature-induced disorder.
The framework will capture the thermal-transport effects of minor oxygen doping.
The framework does not require an empirical Debye temperature.
Existing thermal-transport models conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
Wiedemann–Franz estimates of electronic thermal conductivity can be unreliable and can even yield nonphysical electronic conductivities larger than total conductivity.
The method will remain accurate for oxygen contents up to 1 wt.%.
Accuracy may decline below 50 K or at oxygen impurity levels substantially above 1 wt.%.
The exact error reduction may vary because low-temperature component-separation data are limited.
Deviation exceeding approximately 20% from measurements across the test range, or failure to distinguish electronic and lattice components, will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The performance claim is a roughly 20% relative error reduction versus traditional models, whereas the falsification threshold is a 20% absolute deviation from experiment. These are different metrics, so the stated rule does not decisively test the claimed comparative improvement.

The 10–17 W/(K m) target is presented alongside a 50–1200 K applicability range, without restricting that target to the high-temperature interval from which it was drawn. This creates ambiguity about whether the same conductivity range is predicted below 300 K.
